adare-manor.intro: Adare Manor occupies a nineteenth-century Gothic Revival manor on the River Maigue in Co. Limerick, expanded in 2017 from 62 to 104 rooms and now the golf estate preparing to host the 2027 Ryder Cup. Evidence gathered elsewhere in this research places it as the only demonstrably year-round European estate hotel in the wider comparable set that clears £1,000 a night, which is why it sits in this cohort at all: Fawley underwrites the same figure on the same 365-day calendar. Its ownership structure means the comparison can only run one way. Adare's rate is public; its trading never will be.
record: Adare, Co. Limerick, Ireland; an 840-acre estate on the River Maigue, with an 18-hole golf course

104 rooms and suites: 62 in the Manor House and River Wing (the pre-2017 total), plus 42 in a West Wing added in the 2017 expansion. Planning approval has reportedly been granted for 10 further guest lodges (2025 press); not yet built

Nineteenth-century Gothic Revival manor built from 1832, largely complete by the 1860s, for the 2nd Earl of Dunraven, Windham Henry Quin, and Lady Caroline Wyndham, with work by architects James Pain, Augustus Pugin and Philip Charles Hardwick. A protected structure on Limerick City and County Council's Record of Protected Structures; Buildings of Ireland (NIAH) reference 21824060

Bought by JP McManus and family in December 2014 (some press dates it 2015), reported at about €30m. Operated through Tizzard Holdings Unlimited Company, Irish Companies Registration Office no. 552867, which as an unlimited company is not required to file detailed annual accounts. BDO auditors' reports lodged for the company confirm a loss in each of the three years to FY2025 on a going-concern basis, without disclosing turnover, loss or employee figures

An 18-month restoration and expansion, closing the hotel through 2016-17 and reopening in November 2017, is reported at figures ranging from about €30m to over €100m depending on the source; no single authoritative figure was confirmed. Separately, the estate's course has been rebuilt by architect Tom Fazio ahead of the 2027 Ryder Cup at a reported cost of about €2m a hole (about €36m for 18 holes), alongside government spending reported at €58m towards hosting costs plus a separately funded €150m Adare bypass, both outside the hotel's own capital account

No turnover, loss amount or employee figure has ever entered the public record for this property. BDO's auditors' reports, lodged annually with the Companies Registration Office, confirm losses in FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 while affirming the business remains a going concern; no P&L is filed, since Tizzard Holdings is an unlimited company
Revas Spa, on the east bank of the River Maigue, with 18 treatment rooms, a relaxation pool and a thermal suite
The Oak Room, Michelin-starred since October 2019 and the only Michelin star in Co. Limerick, under chef Michael Tweedie; also Ōku (Japanese) and The Carriage House, a restaurant, bar and terrace
Weddings from a minimum of 150 guests, with the Grand Ballroom holding up to 320; exclusive whole-Manor-House buyouts offered for private celebrations, price not published
cards: What happened

JP McManus and family bought the hotel in December 2014 for a reported €30m, then closed it for an 18-month restoration and expansion that added a West Wing built as a limestone replica of the original block, raising the room count from 62 to 104 and adding a ballroom, reopening in November 2017. Reported costs for that programme range from about €30m to over €100m depending on the source, with no single figure confirmed in sources found. The estate's golf course has since been rebuilt by Tom Fazio ahead of hosting the 2027 Ryder Cup, backed by government funding reported at €58m towards hosting costs on top of the owner's own course investment.
What it earns

Adare Manor is operated through Tizzard Holdings Unlimited Company, which as an Irish unlimited company is not required to file a profit and loss account. What is public is narrower than a number: BDO's auditors' reports, lodged each year with the Companies Registration Office, confirm the company made a loss in FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 while affirming the business remains a going concern. No turnover, loss amount or employee figure has ever entered the public record for this property, in filed accounts or in press estimates found.
What it evidences for Fawley

Adare is the closest thing in the comparable set to an existence proof for Fawley's central bet: a year-round European estate hotel clearing roughly £1,000 a night on the lead-in evidence held. But its trading will never be tested against Fawley's own filed-accounts comparators, because its ownership structure keeps the number out of the public record entirely. The strongest rate evidence in the set arrives with the weakest financial disclosure, so it can confirm that the rate is achievable in the market but cannot confirm what margin, if any, it produces.

aman-rosa-alpina.intro: Aman Rosa Alpina occupies a village site in San Cassiano, in the Alta Badia valley of the Dolomites, at just over 1,500 metres. A family-run hotel since 1939, it closed for a full rebuild under an Aman partnership agreed in November 2020 and reopened in July 2025 with 51 suites, a new spa and two dining outlets. It sits in the comparable set on the strength of a press-reported rate uplift after that rebuild, testing Fawley Court's underwritten cost base and margin against a comparably scaled European mountain property.

amanzoe.intro: Amanzoe sits on a hilltop above Porto Heli in the eastern Peloponnese, built from nothing as a purpose-designed Aman resort rather than a restoration of an existing house. It is the comparable set's clearest case of a rate this high running alongside a substantial branded-villa programme sold to owners who also draw on the hotel's own facilities, the same hospitality-plus-residences shape Fawley proposes to build. It carries no heritage designation and no conversion story; what it tests is whether resort scale, brand and a defined summer season can sustain ultra-luxury rates without a country-house history behind them.
record: Porto Heli, eastern Peloponnese, Greece; a hilltop resort covering about 93 hectares (230 acres) overlooking the Argolic Gulf

Reported as around 40 independent pavilions plus a smaller number of stand-alone villas at the 2012 launch (the developer's own account); current listings show 38 standard Pavilions, 3 Beach Pavilions and up to 12 villas, though sources vary on the exact current villa count

Developed by Dolphin Capital Investors and designed by architect Ed Tuttle, opening August 2012. Grivalia Hospitality (85%) and Dolphin Capital Partners (15%) bought 100% of the resort in August 2018 for €5.8m cash plus assumption of €76.5m of debt, about €82.3m all-in and an implied €116m enterprise value; the same deal committed the purchasers to buy 20 plots at the adjacent Kilada Hills project for €10m. Aman Resorts operates the property under a management contract

Reported at almost €100m invested by the August 2012 launch, part funded by a Bank of Cyprus loan (press, 2012). Against roughly 40-50 keys this implies very roughly €2m-2.5m a key, computed; the figure spans the whole resort and villas together and predates any refurbishment since, so it is not a clean per-key comparator

Grivalia Hospitality SA, the group that owns Amanzoe, reported group revenue of €44.0m and an operating (EBIT) loss of about €47.5m for FY2023, with net losses continuing into FY2024 at about €54m. These are group-wide figures across Grivalia's wider hospitality portfolio, not an Amanzoe-only profit and loss account, so should not be read as the resort's own margin

Nine treatment rooms across five indoor and two outdoor spa suites plus a dedicated facial room, a Watsu aquatic-therapy pool, hydrotherapy areas (saunas, hammams, steam rooms, cold pools), a gym, yoga pavilion, Pilates studio and two tennis courts
Multiple outlets including a main restaurant, an open-air amphitheatre dining experience, a pool restaurant and a beach-club restaurant; no Michelin recognition found
The resort markets weddings and private celebrations through its own 'Celebrations' programme; no published capacity or price found

Branded villas sold as Aman Residences: one-bedroom units from about $3.6m, two-bedroom from about €3.2m, four-bedroom from about €6.5m; owners hold privileged access to the resort's dining, spa and beach-club facilities
cards: What happened

Dolphin Capital Investors developed the resort from undeveloped hilltop land, with architect Ed Tuttle, opening it as the first Aman-branded resort in Europe to integrate branded villas in August 2012. Ownership consolidated in August 2018 when Grivalia Hospitality and Dolphin Capital Partners bought out the remaining interest for about €82.3m, a €5.8m cash payment plus assumption of €76.5m of debt, implying a €116m enterprise value. Aman Resorts continues to operate the property under a management contract; there is no conversion or restoration story, since the resort was built new rather than adapted from an existing structure.
What it earns

Amanzoe's own FY2023 turnover of €41.80m, on a perimeter that includes villa sales, is already held elsewhere in this research, as are its achieved rate and one season's occupancy. What research for this page adds is the parent picture: Grivalia Hospitality SA, the group that owns Amanzoe, reported €44.0m of group revenue and an operating loss of about €47.5m for FY2023, with net losses continuing into FY2024 at about €54m. Those figures span Grivalia's wider portfolio, not Amanzoe alone, so they cannot be read as the resort's own margin, but they show a group investing heavily and still running at a loss even as its flagship resort trades at scale.
What it evidences for Fawley

Amanzoe combines an achieved rate well above Fawley's £1,000 underwrite with a defined roughly seven-and-a-half-month season, against Fawley's 365-day calendar, and a villa-sales limb that has been running since 2012. It is evidence that a hospitality-plus-residences model can work at this rate level over a long season. It is not evidence that it produces a profit at group level: the parent company's continuing losses argue against assuming that revenue scale and brand alone secure margin, which is the same caution the Fawley underwrite already carries in its own GOP assumptions.

ballyfin-demesne.intro: Ballyfin trades from a single Regency mansion at the centre of a 614-acre demesne in the Irish midlands, restored over roughly nine years by its American owners before opening as a twenty-key hotel. It is the smallest hotel in the comparable set and the only one whose Irish filed accounts break turnover down by department, which is why a genuinely representative achieved room rate exists for it at all, rather than a published or quoted figure. That disclosure is the reason it sits in the cohort: it is the one place the gap between an advertised rate and what a comparable actually collects can be measured rather than assumed.
record: Ballyfin, Co. Laois, Ireland; a 614-acre private demesne in the Slieve Bloom foothills, landscaped in the Regency period

20 rooms and suites in the main house (5 suites, 8 staterooms, 7 deluxe rooms, 1 single and 2 ground-floor rooms on one published breakdown), plus a separate Gardener's Cottage; 21 keys including the cottage on the hotel's own count

Neoclassical mansion built 1821-26 for Sir Charles Coote, 9th Baronet, to designs by Sir Richard Morrison and his son William Vitruvius Morrison, replacing an earlier house of 1778; NIAH reference 12801204 (Buildings of Ireland)

Bought as a derelict former school (Patrician College) in 2002 by Chicago businessman Fred Krehbiel and his wife Kay; restored over roughly nine years and opened as a hotel in May 2011. Fred Krehbiel died suddenly in June 2021; the family, led by sons Jay and Liam, has stated it remains committed to the property. Operating company: Ballyfin Demesne Limited, Irish Companies Registration Office no. 355480
Press reports cite about $50m spent on the restoration by the 2011 opening, with no split published between acquisition and works; no more recent capital figure was found

FY2024 filed accounts (Ballyfin Demesne Limited, Companies Registration Office): turnover €6.61m, down from €6.85m in FY2023, of which accommodation revenue was about €4.0m (down from about €4.3m), food and beverage €1.95m and other revenue €647k. Loss after tax €389,281, up from €90,155 in FY2023. 96 employees, up from 93, with staff costs rising by about €300,000 over the year
Indoor swimming pool, sauna, steam room and treatment rooms; no size or treatment-room count published

One Michelin star in the 2026 Guide, Republic of Ireland; Executive Chef Richard Picard-Edwards, previously of the Mandarin Oriental, London. Dining held in the State Dining Room and Turner Conservatory, with a separate Cellar Bar and wine cellar
Exclusive whole-house buyouts offered for weddings and private celebrations; no published buyout price found
cards: What happened

Fred and Kay Krehbiel bought the estate derelict in 2002, then the former Patrician College boys' school, itself a repurposing of the neoclassical Regency mansion the Morrisons built in 1821-26 for Sir Charles Coote. They spent roughly nine years and a reported $50m restoring it, working with historians, conservators and Irish landscape designer Jim Reynolds, before opening as a 20-suite hotel in May 2011. Fred Krehbiel died in 2021; his sons have said the family remains committed to the property, which continues to trade under its original restoration ownership rather than having changed hands.
What it earns

FY2024 filed accounts show turnover of €6.61m, down from €6.85m the year before, driven mainly by a fall in accommodation revenue from about €4.3m to €4.0m. The hotel made a loss after tax of €389,281, more than four times the €90,155 loss in FY2023, as staff costs rose by roughly €300,000 to cover a headcount that grew from 93 to 96. This is a hotel at Fawley's rate class making a filed loss even after fourteen years of trading, on a business small enough (96 staff against 20-21 keys, about 4.6-4.8 a key) that the fixed cost of running a house this size falls on relatively few room-nights.
What it evidences for Fawley

Ballyfin carries the comparable set's only derived achieved room rate, about £762, against a published seasonal package of €1,390-1,760, which is the clearest evidence anywhere in this research of the gap between an advertised rate and what a comparable actually collects; Fawley underwrites £1,000 flat. Ballyfin's FY2024 loss, on a 20-key hotel trading almost year-round at about 344 days, also weighs against any assumption that rate alone secures profitability at this end of the market, since Ballyfin sits above every UK comparable on rate and is still filing a loss.

beaverbrook.intro: Longshot bought Cherkley Court — built in 1866 for the wool manufacturer Abraham Dixon and later, for fifty years, Lord Beaverbrook's home — in 2011, and opened it in stages rather than at once: the Garden House and its restaurant first, in October 2016, the Grade II-listed main house the following year, and a fourth building, a 21-suite village, only in 2024. Financing followed the same order: the estate's only disclosed facility, a £52m loan from OakNorth, arrived in January 2024, thirteen years after acquisition and well after the hotel had a trading record to borrow against. It stands in the set as the closest UK precedent for a country-house conversion carried out in phases and at a comparable scale to Fawley Court, on an estate without Fawley's own park designation.
record_extra: Ownership

Freehold held via Longshot Cherkley Court Ltd, renamed Beaverbrook Holdings Limited in 2021 (company 07457718, incorporated 2 December 2010); acquired by Longshot, led by Joel Cadbury and Ollie Vigors, in 2011
Trading

Filed by Beaverbrook Holdings Limited (company 07457718) for the year to 31 March 2025: turnover £28.85m, adjusted EBITDA £3.60m (a 12.5% margin) and payroll at 45.6% of revenue on 462 average employees — this supersedes the case study's existing 'no property-level filed accounts located' line; see conflicts
Heritage and history

Built 1866–1870 for the wool manufacturer Abraham Dixon; bought by Max Aitken (later Lord Beaverbrook) in 1910 for £30,000, who spent a further £10,000 in 1911 on electricity, heating, a swimming pool and one of Britain's first home cinemas; his widow held the estate until her death in 1994; it reopened to the public in 2007 after restoration, before Longshot's 2011 acquisition
What happened, in sequence

Phased opening: the Garden House (11 rooms, a 55-seat restaurant and a cookery school) opened October 2016; the Grade II-listed main House (18 rooms) opened in 2017; a spa followed later in 2017; the Village (21 suites) opened 2024, funded by the £52m OakNorth facility of January 2024
conflicts: The existing case-study record states 'No property-level filed accounts located; the trading entity files within a group.' Beaverbrook Holdings Limited (company 07457718, formerly Longshot Cherkley Court Ltd) does file standalone accounts: the year to 31 March 2025 shows turnover £28.85m, adjusted EBITDA £3.60m (12.5% margin) and payroll at 45.6% of revenue on 462 average employees — already carried in the portal's own held figures panel for this property (margin, payroll, capex), but not reflected in the case-study text.

The existing case-study record states the hotel 'opened in phases from August 2017.' The first phase, the 11-room Garden House with its restaurant and cookery school, opened in October 2016 — about ten months earlier. The Grade II-listed main House followed in 2017, which is presumably the date the existing text refers to.

A 2024 press report on the OakNorth facility (The Business Magazine) describes Beaverbrook as a '57-room hotel' at that date, one more than the 56 keys (house 18, garden 11, coach house 6, village 21) already held. This may be a rounding or snapshot difference; it is noted, not resolved.

belmond-castello-di-casole.intro: Castello di Casole sits on a large hilltop estate in the Tuscan countryside near Siena, developed from 2005 as a combined hotel and residential project before Belmond bought it in 2018. The filed Italian company behind it is registered for dealing in its own real estate, not as a pure hotel operator, because the estate still carries an active programme of restored farmhouses and villas sold to private buyers alongside the hotel. It belongs in this set because it tests a question Fawley Court's own structure raises directly: what a country-house hotel conversion looks like once a residential-sales limb is layered onto it, and what happens to that limb when it does not sell out on the hotel's own timeline.
record: A hilltop estate of roughly 1,450 to 1,500 hectares near Casole d'Elsa, Siena province, Tuscany
41 suites at the hotel's 2012 opening; 39 suites currently marketed, plus two private hotel villas, Villa Thesan and Villa Usil, opened for the 2024 season

Developed from 2005 by Timbers Resorts with SV Capital and the Antonello family; the hotel opened 1 July 2012; Belmond (now LVMH) bought the estate in February 2018 for total consideration of €40.2m, a share purchase of the two Italian companies that owned it

Filed as Castello di Casole S.p.A., classified under Italy's ATECO code for dealing in own real estate, not as a pure hotel company; its stated corporate objects cover construction, renovation and sale of buildings alongside hotel and agricultural activity
FY2024 filed turnover €14.549m and a net loss of €3.510m; FY2023 turnover €12.645m and a net loss of €192k; no EBITDA is disclosed

€40.2m, February 2018: €38.287m cash plus €1.003m contingent consideration (later lapsed) plus €0.903m acquisition costs; purchase accounting allocated roughly €22.6m to hotel land and buildings and roughly €22.6m to unsold residential land

Originally a 48-plot residential programme of restored and newly built casali and villas; 15 to 16 plots remained unsold at Belmond's 2018 acquisition; the balance is still marketed today as “Casali di Casole” by the original developer, separately from the hotel, with 31 residences cited at a 2019 relaunch
Essere Spa, set in a former wine cellar: sauna, steam room and a hydro-massage pool, open daily 10:00 to 19:00
Four outlets: Tosca, Castello Grill, Emporio del Castello and Bar Visconti, alongside a historic wine cellar used for tastings and private dining
cards: What happened

The estate was developed from 2005 by Timbers Resorts, in partnership with SV Capital and the Antonello family, as a mixed hotel and residential project: restored and newly built casali and villas for sale, alongside a conversion of the medieval castle into a boutique hotel. The hotel opened on 1 July 2012 as a 41-suite property, later than early marketing had suggested. Belmond bought the estate in February 2018 for total consideration of €40.2m, structured as a share purchase of the two Italian companies that owned it. Purchase accounting split that price roughly evenly: about €22.6m to the hotel's land and buildings, and about €22.6m to unsold residential land, confirming the deal bought a residential land bank as much as it bought a hotel.
What it earns

The filed entity, Castello di Casole S.p.A., is not a hotel-only profit and loss account. It is registered for dealing in its own real estate, and its corporate objects span construction, renovation and sale of buildings as well as hotel and agricultural activity. FY2024 turnover was €14.5m, close to FY2023's €12.6m, and the entity made a net loss in both years: €3.5m in 2024, €0.2m in 2023. No EBITDA is disclosed. Because the entity carries residential-plot activity alongside hotel operations, this turnover figure cannot be read as a hotel revenue comparator without an adjustment that no public source supports.
What it evidences for Fawley

The transferable point is scope, not rate. Casole shows a country-house hotel conversion that did not stand alone commercially: the vendor built out a 48-unit residential programme alongside the hotel, and 15 to 16 of those units were still unsold when Belmond bought the estate, six years after the hotel opened, with the remainder still being marketed by a separate developer in 2026. Fawley's own case pairs a 60-key hotel with twelve branded residences on comparable logic, residential sales supporting a return the hotel alone may not carry, with the residential limb running on its own execution timeline. Casole's filed accounts cannot supply a hotel margin or revenue-a-key comparator against Fawley's £756k Year 7 revenue a key or 33.96% GOP, because the entity mixes hotel and property-dealing income; that gap should travel with any citation of the Casole figures.

belmond-hotel-cipriani.intro: Belmond Hotel Cipriani occupies the eastern tip of Giudecca, an island with no natural footfall of its own, reachable from Venice only by the hotel's private launch across the lagoon. Giuseppe Cipriani, of Harry's Bar, opened it in 1958 and it has passed through three ownership eras since: a family sale in 1967, a corporate purchase in 1976 that became Orient-Express Hotels and then Belmond, and LVMH's 2019 acquisition of the whole Belmond portfolio. It sits in this comparable set at the top of the rate ladder, the highest lead-in rate held anywhere in the cohort, and it is the evidence for how lean payroll can run at that end of the market.
record: 79 rooms and suites: 63 in the main Cipriani building, 16 in the adjoining 15th-century Palazzo Vendramin. The count has fallen from 102 keys in 2001; an older, widely repeated figure of 96 keys is dated and should not be used without a vintage qualifier

Palazzo Vendramin is described by the hotel as 15th-century; the main Cipriani building was constructed 1956–58. No individually confirmed cultural-heritage designation was established for either building under Italy's Codice dei beni culturali, a diligence gap rather than evidence of no protection

Initiated in 1956 by Giuseppe Cipriani in collaboration with Lord Iveagh and the Guinness family, opened 1958; Cipriani sold his interest in 1967; a Sea Containers group company bought Hotel Cipriani SRL in 1976 for £900,000; the business became Orient-Express Hotels, rebranded Belmond in 2014; LVMH completed its acquisition of Belmond on 17 April 2019 for a $3.2bn enterprise value across 45 properties, with no Cipriani-specific price disclosed

A documented $3m programme upgraded 16 rooms in the San Giorgio and Redentore wings, November 2007 to March 2008, the only disclosed refurbishment cost. A current Peter Marino-led renovation opened its first phase, a new lobby and 13 redesigned rooms, in May 2025, with a new Dior Spa following in July 2026; no budget has been published for either phase

FY2001 RevPAR of US$592 (on 102 keys then); FY2007 RevPAR growth of 18%; a Q1 2016 RevPAR swing of +58% year on year, driven by the Easter calendar rather than underlying demand. No property-level achieved rate or occupancy has been disclosed since Belmond delisted from public markets in 2019

The former Casanova Wellness Centre offered three treatment rooms plus one couples room, a hair salon, a Technogym fitness room, sauna and steam room; no floor area was published. It has since been superseded by the Dior Spa Hotel Cipriani, opened July 2026, across two floors with five treatment rooms including one double. The hotel's separate outdoor seawater pool is heated and filtered, 33m by 13.5m

Five outlets: Oro, holding one Michelin star, with Head Chef Vania Ghedini and Massimo Bottura as Culinary Creative Director; Cip's Club, led by chef Roberto Gatto; Il Porticciolo; Gabbiano Bar; and Bacaro Dior

Two ballrooms seat up to 340 guests combined; ceremony sites include Casanova Garden (250 guests) and Antique Garden (120 guests). Full exclusive-use hire is offered but no whole-hotel buyout price is published. Published venue hire runs from €5,000 (San Giorgio Terrace, Antique Garden) to €22,000 for both ballrooms together, VAT included, setups extra

cards: What happened

Giuseppe Cipriani, of Harry's Bar, opened the hotel in 1958 on Giudecca, an island the hotel itself had to make reachable with a private launch service across the lagoon, then and now part of the guest experience. Cipriani sold his interest in 1967; Sea Containers bought the operating company in 1976 for £900,000 and folded it into what became Orient-Express Hotels, renamed Belmond in 2014. LVMH bought Belmond in April 2019 for $3.2bn across the whole 45-property portfolio, with no price disclosed for Cipriani individually. The hotel has been refurbished in phases rather than once: a documented $3m programme in 2007–08, further unpriced work through the 2000s, and a current Peter Marino-led renovation whose first phase, a new lobby and 13 rooms, opened in May 2025, with a new Dior Spa following in 2026.
What it earns

The filed basis already held for this hotel, €431k revenue a key and 18.1% payroll, the lowest payroll ratio in this set, describes a small, expensive-to-run hotel operating at scale rates few comparables reach. The only additional achieved-performance evidence found predates Belmond's 2019 delisting: RevPAR of $592 in FY2001, on 102 keys then; +18% RevPAR growth in FY2007; and a +58% RevPAR swing in Q1 2016, driven by the Easter calendar rather than underlying demand. No property-level rate or occupancy has been disclosed publicly since Belmond left public markets.
What it evidences for Fawley

Cipriani's 18.1% filed payroll ratio, the lowest in the whole comparable set, sits well below the 22.4% direct-departmental-wages figure the Fawley model carries; but Cipriani's keys count has fallen from 102 in 2001 to 79 today, and an ultra-small, ultra-high-rate operation can run lean on payroll in a way a 60-key hotel with twelve residences and Fawley's fuller amenity programme may not replicate. The lead-in rate held for Cipriani, £2,011 gross, sits roughly double Fawley's £1,000 underwrite, but Cipriani earns that on a season of roughly seven and a half months against Fawley's 365-day calendar. The comparison is a ceiling on achievable rate, not a benchmark for annual revenue a key.

belmond-hotel-splendido.intro: Splendido occupies a hillside above Portofino harbour, built as a Benedictine monastery in the sixteenth century before becoming a private summer residence and later a hotel, now owned by LVMH within the Belmond collection. It reopened in June 2025 after a phased, multi-year renovation, and it sits in this set as one of the highest-rate coastal comparables Fawley is bracketed against -- with a season question the portal's own research had left open, and which this page settles.
record: Portofino, Italian Riviera, Liguria, Italy -- Viale Baratta 16, on the hillside above the harbour

Belmond's own site states 48 rooms and suites plus 5 signature suites plus 1 independent private villa (Villa Beatrice) -- 54 accommodations in total. A free Italian filed-accounts aggregator gives 61 rooms instead, from an unverified company profile -- a genuine, unreconciled conflict between the operator's own count and the registry profile

Part of Belmond, wholly owned by LVMH. The filed Italian entity is Hotel Splendido S.p.A. (P.IVA 00169400991, REA GE-218366). No separate management contract was found, consistent with direct group ownership and operation

A phased, multi-year renovation by Martin Brudnizki Design Studio: the pool, the Splendido Grill and the Baronessa Suite were redesigned in 2023; the lobby and most rooms were refreshed in 2024; the hotel made its grand reopening on 7 June 2025 with a new Dior Spa and a redesigned Baratta Sedici Bar. No total renovation cost has been disclosed -- older, non-comparable 2018 disclosures of USD 2.4m and USD 5.3m predate this renovation by more than six years and should not be used for it

Filed entity Hotel Splendido S.p.A.: turnover fell from EUR 45.875m (FY2022) to EUR 39.199m (FY2023) to EUR 34.441m (FY2024), alongside a EUR 1.578m net loss and EUR 8.329m staff cost (24.2% of turnover) in FY2024 -- both held. Employee counts conflict sharply across sources: 50-99 (one FY2024 aggregator), 175 (a FY2023 profile) and 330 (a current 2026 directory field)

Villa Beatrice: a separately branded, century-old clifftop private-use villa a short walk from the hotel, launched July 2025. Sleeps up to 10 guests across 5 keys; exclusive-use only, on its own shorter season (29 June - 2 November in its 2025 debut year), pricing on request. A rental product, not a sale
cards: What happened

Splendido began as a 16th-century Benedictine monastery before becoming the Baron Baratta family's summer residence in the 19th century, and later a hotel that became part of Belmond's collection, now wholly owned by LVMH. The most recent chapter is a phased, multi-year renovation by Martin Brudnizki Design Studio: the pool, the Splendido Grill and the Baronessa Suite were redesigned in 2023, the lobby and most rooms were refreshed in 2024, and the hotel made its grand reopening on 7 June 2025 with a new Dior Spa, a redesigned Baratta Sedici Bar, and the launch of Villa Beatrice, a separate clifftop private villa nearby. No total cost for the renovation has been disclosed.
What it earns

The filed entity, Hotel Splendido S.p.A., shows a declining revenue run through the renovation years: turnover fell from EUR 45.875m (FY2022) to EUR 39.199m (FY2023) to EUR 34.441m (FY2024), alongside a EUR 1.578m net loss and staff cost of EUR 8.329m (24.2% of turnover) in FY2024. That pattern is consistent with a hotel absorbing renovation disruption across the period, though no filed note confirms the causal link. Employee counts conflict sharply across sources -- 50-99, 175 and 330 all appear in different registry profiles for different years -- and no EBITDA, GOP or occupancy figure was found anywhere.
What it evidences for Fawley

The most useful finding here is not a headline figure but a correction to the season the portal held. Belmond's own live SynXis booking calendar, collected as part of this desk's own rate collection on 18 August 2026, shows the hotel bookable continuously (aside from individually sold-out nights) from before the collection window through 1 November 2026, closing 2 November 2026 and reopening 5 March 2027 -- a season of roughly nine months, not the four-month '8 June to 29 September' window one third-party listing claimed, and consistent with the 'closes 2 November' figure the other listing gave. On trading, the post-renovation entity is currently loss-making at a 24.2% payroll ratio against Fawley's 22.4% direct-departmental-wages figure -- not a like-for-like comparison, but a reminder that a fully renovated, ultra-high-rate Riviera hotel can still show a filed loss in a heavy capex year.

belmond-villa-san-michele.intro: Belmond Villa San Michele occupies a former Franciscan monastery on the hillside above Fiesole, looking down over Florence. Orient-Express, Belmond's predecessor, bought the property in 1982, and it has traded as a hotel since, most recently closing for an eighteen-month restyling before reopening on 28 April 2026 with a smaller room count, a new spa and a new restaurant. It sits in the comparable set as one of the few Italian estate hotels with a genuine, property-specific filed accounts trail, and that trail shows a hotel that lost money in the year running into its closure.
record: Fiesole, in the hills above Florence, within a terraced park of cypress and olive most listing sources put at around 16 hectares; a precise, independently verified acreage was not found in a primary source (aggregated hotel and venue listings, e.g. bellinitravel.com, willowandoakevents.com).

39 rooms and suites after the 2026 reopening; older sources and the brief's own working assumption cite a larger, roughly 45-key count from before the restyling, which is now superseded (lvmh.com press release, 20 May 2026; noted conflict in the deal's own prior research).

Founded as a Franciscan monastery around 1413 on land donated by the Florentine Davanzati family; enlarged and rebuilt in 1599-1600 under Santi di Tito, financed by Giovanni di Bartolomeo Davanzati, giving the villa the facade traditionally attributed to Michelangelo and the loggia that survives today (aggregated historical sources, e.g. italiaatavola.net, histouring.com; the Michelangelo attribution is described in every source found as traditional/reputed, not documented).

Bought by Orient-Express (Belmond's predecessor) in 1982; consideration and seller not found. Now held within LVMH/Belmond through Villa San Michele S.p.A., a 100%-controlled Italian entity (P.IVA/CF 00546220484, REA FI-118471, Florence chamber of commerce, ATECO 55.1 hotel accommodation) (belmond press kit; LVMH FY2024 consolidated accounts).

A press-reported EUR 30m, eighteen-month restyling, 2024-26, covering rooms, spa, gardens and restaurant - about EUR 769,000 (about GBP 660,000) a key on the 39 reopened rooms. This figure is already held by the portal; it is carried here for the record only (t24economia.it, 2024 press estimate).

Filed at Villa San Michele S.p.A.: FY2024 turnover EUR 14.368m and a net loss of EUR 7.453m (about GBP 6.39m at EUR1=GBP0.8575) - the loss figure is already held by the portal. The filed turnover series behind it shows a hotel still ramping from a low base: EUR 1.708m (FY2020), EUR 5.333m (FY2021), EUR 12.602m (FY2022), EUR 10.847m (FY2023), EUR 14.368m (FY2024). EBITDA, GOP, staff cost and filed headcount are not disclosed (topaziende.quotidiano.net; ufficiocamerale.it).
A new Spa by Guerlain opened with the 2026 reopening, entered through a 'Secret Garden', with hand-painted murals by Elena Carozzi; treatment-room count and area not found (lvmh.com press release).
A new restaurant, Antesi, opened with the 2026 reopening; no Michelin recognition was found, and no second outlet or bar was identified in this research (lvmh.com press release).

Indoor and outdoor spaces advertised for weddings and events for 20 to 200 guests: the Cenacolo Room for up to 50 and the Davanzati Room, with its own private garden, for up to 100 (willowandoakevents.com).
cards: What happened

The monastery on this site dates to around 1413, was enlarged in 1599-1600 with the facade traditionally attributed to Michelangelo, and was bought by Orient-Express in 1982. It traded as a hotel for over four decades before closing for an eighteen-month, press-reported EUR 30m restyling that touched the rooms, gardens, spa and restaurant. It reopened on 28 April 2026 with 39 rooms and suites, down from a larger pre-renovation count, a new Guerlain spa and a new restaurant, Antesi.
What it earns

The only filed trading year available, FY2024, shows turnover of EUR 14.368m and a net loss of EUR 7.453m - a bottom-line result, not an EBITDA or GOP figure, and one earned in a year that included part of the run-up to an eighteen-month closure. The turnover series behind it (EUR 1.7m in 2020 rising to EUR 14.4m in 2024) reads as a hotel still recovering scale after the pandemic, not a stabilised trading year; no post-reopening figures exist yet.
What it evidences for Fawley

Even before its 2026 renovation, this Michelangelo-attributed monastery above Florence was turning over about EUR 368,000 (roughly GBP 316,000) a key and still losing EUR 7.45m - well under half of Fawley's underwritten GBP 737,881 a key, on a filed net result rather than GOP. Its capex, at a press-reported GBP 660,000 a key for a full restyling of an existing hotel, sits far below Fawley's GBP 2.06m a key for a ground-up conversion of a much larger estate, which is the more useful half of the comparison: the capex gap is explained by scope, but the revenue and trading gap is a genuine warning sign from the closest thing to a like-for-like Italian estate hotel with real filed numbers.

castello-di-reschio.intro: Castello di Reschio occupies a large private estate in the hills of Umbria, close to the Tuscan border, where a ruined medieval castle has been restored into a hotel by the family that has owned and been rebuilding the wider estate for three decades. The restoration paired the castle conversion with a parallel programme of restoring outlying farmhouses for freehold sale, a residential-sales limb run alongside the hotel rather than through it. It sits in this comparable set because it brackets Fawley Court on both counts: a listed-heritage hotel conversion on an estate large enough to carry its own residential programme, within the same European ceiling cohort against which Fawley's rate and capital cost are being tested.
record_extra: Heritage

Listed under Italy's Cultural Heritage and Landscape Code: the castle appears as beneficiary "Bolza Antonius Benedikt" in the Ministry of Culture's 2019 funding programme for protected heritage assets, and the restoration contractor classifies the work as OG2, the category for restoration of protected immovable heritage. No specific decree or catalogue register number was found
Capital cost

The 2019 Ministry funding programme discloses €8,855,681.33 of total works for Castello di Reschio, with a proposed 15% public contribution of €1,328,352.20. This is a funding-scheme figure covering the wider 2015–2020 restoration, about 10,500 sqm across the castle, spa, restaurant, church, pool and stables, not a hotel-only conversion cost, so no defensible cost a key can be drawn from it
Villas to rent

Eight former-farmhouse casali are currently listed as rentable estate villas: Palmieri, Cercoschene, Bell'Aria, Spinaltermine, Tisciano, Barco, Piantaverna and Arrighi, separate from the roughly 36-key hotel and from the wider stock of over 50 restored farmhouses on the estate
Residences

The residential model is freehold whole-house sale, not a club or fractional interest. A 2023 interview with Benedikt Bolza put 28 of 50 houses as restored and sold, at prices that had moved from an indicative €4m–€7m in 2016 to around €10m by 2023, both dated indications rather than a current price list
Membership
No club, membership programme or joining fee was found. Riding, dressage and tennis are offered as estate services to hotel and villa guests rather than through a member-owned club
Michelin

The hotel holds Three MICHELIN Keys, the guide's hotel-quality award, not a restaurant star. No Michelin-star recognition was found for either of its two restaurants, Ristorante al Castello and Ristorante alle Scuderie

castiglion-del-bosco.intro: Castiglion del Bosco sits on a 2,000-hectare estate in Montalcino, inside the Val d'Orcia UNESCO World Heritage Site, combining a 42-suite borgo hotel, eleven guest villas, a Brunello di Montalcino winery and Italy's only private golf club. It carries the highest revenue a key in the whole comparable set, ahead of Fawley's own Year 7 underwrite, which makes establishing what that revenue actually covers -- hotel rooms alone, or the wider estate -- the central question this page has to answer.
record: Montalcino, Tuscany, inside the Val d'Orcia UNESCO World Heritage Site; a c.2,000-hectare (c.5,000-acre) estate, mostly woodland and a wildlife reserve, with 62 hectares under Sangiovese vine; c.45km (28 miles) from Siena, c.89km (55 miles) from Florence

42 suites in the borgo plus 11 detached guest villas (3-6 bedrooms, private heated pools, converted from 17th-18th century farmhouses) -- 53 accommodation units in total; an earlier phase offered 23 suites before the borgo's expansion

900-plus years of estate history, with 12th-13th century castle ruins and the medieval church of Pieve San Michele (c.725 AD) on the grounds; no formal listing register number was found for any structure

Massimo and Chiara Ferragamo bought the estate in 2003; sold in March 2022 to an unnamed international family office, press-estimated at EUR 300m-400m for the whole estate (hotel, winery, golf and other assets together, not a hotel-only price); Rosewood Hotels & Resorts has managed the hotel since 2015 (the management contract's term and fee basis were not found)

Restoration began after the 2003 acquisition; the golf course was completed in 2010; no conversion or restoration cost figure was found for the hotel -- and none should be derived from the 2022 whole-estate sale price

2026 season (from 21 March): Junior Suite EUR 1,450 low season / EUR 2,050 high season -- but the quoted rate includes daily breakfast (and a car for villa stays), so it is not directly comparable to a room-only lead-in

Filed entity Castiglion del Bosco Hotel S.r.l. (P.IVA 01194630529): FY2024 turnover EUR 45.074m, net profit EUR 3.575m, filed under ATECO 55.1 (hotels). Staff cost EUR 8.755m on 241 employees per one free-registry aggregator; a second aggregator gives 175 employees -- a genuine, unresolved conflict in the free evidence

Spa built into the borgo's former wine cellars, with sauna, steam bath, relaxation area and a private garden; two treatment lines (Officina Profumo Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella; EviDenS de Beaute); treatment-room count not found

Ristorante Campo del Drago: two Michelin stars (first awarded 2023, second 2025), chef Matteo Temperini since 2019. Osteria La Canonica: Tuscan trattoria with wood-fired oven. Plus La Canonica Cooking School and a pool bar
Up to 200 guests for meetings and celebrations; three meeting rooms (8-20 person capacity each); a private villa available for events
The Club at Castiglion del Bosco -- Italy's only private golf club (Tom Weiskopf design, completed 2010) -- family membership, invitation only; joining fee and annual dues not published

The 11 current guest villas are marketed as hotel accommodation, not demonstrated to be privately owned. A historical (2009) scheme targeted 120 residence-club members at a EUR 1m upfront lifetime transferable fee, guaranteeing six weeks' annual use across c.20 villas and borgo apartments; current sell-down numbers, prices and tenure were not found
cards: What happened

The Ferragamo family bought the 2,000-hectare Montalcino estate in 2003 and rebuilt it in phases: the golf course by 2010, the hotel opening from 2008, Rosewood brought in to manage from 2015, and the accommodation count expanding from an original 23 suites to today's 42 suites plus 11 villas. In March 2022 the Ferragamos sold the whole estate -- hotel, winery, golf club and other assets together -- to an unnamed international family office, press-estimated at EUR 300m-400m. No hotel-only consideration, and no conversion capex figure for any phase of the build, has ever been disclosed, so the spend that produced the current resort cannot be benchmarked against Fawley's works budget.
What it earns

The only filed financial evidence is Castiglion del Bosco Hotel S.r.l.'s FY2024 accounts: EUR 45.074m turnover and EUR 3.575m net profit, filed under an ATECO 55.1 hotel classification. That entity is legally and fiscally distinct from Castiglion del Bosco Societa Agricola a r.l. -- the winery, filed separately under ATECO 0121 (grape cultivation), confirmed by its own VAT registration -- so wine sales sit outside the EUR 45.07m figure. Whether the golf club's and the 11 guest villas' income also sit inside that same figure, or accrue to other related entities, is not established from public filings; the entity's hotel-only name and ATECO code are consistent with a hotel-and-villas perimeter but do not prove it. No EBITDA, GOP or occupancy figure is filed or found anywhere.
What it evidences for Fawley

On EUR 45.07m of turnover across 53 accommodation units, revenue a key computes to EUR 850,449 (GBP 729,760 at the deal's FX convention) -- the highest in the whole comparable set, above Fawley's GBP 756k Year 7 underwrite. But that figure almost certainly blends rooms, F&B, spa, golf and event income (no departmental split is disclosed), so it is not a clean rooms-revenue comparison, and the perimeter question is only half-answered: the winery is confirmed out, the golf club and villas are not confirmed either way. The 19.4% payroll figure, on that same broad revenue base, is not comparable to Fawley's 22.4% direct-departmental-wages figure without knowing what activities sit inside each. The quoted EUR 1,450-2,050 Junior Suite rate includes breakfast (and a car for villas), so it overstates the room-only equivalent against Fawley's GBP 1,000 room-only underwrite.

chateau-de-la-messardiere.intro: Chateau de la Messardiere stands on a wooded rise above Saint-Tropez, with views over the bay to the old town. LOV Hotel Collection bought it in 2019 and reopened it as an Airelles house in July 2021 after a two-year renovation. It sits at the top of the wider comparable set on price and margin at once: the highest lead-in rate found in this research and one of only two properties in the whole cohort with a filed EBITDA margin above 35%, on a season of about five and a half months, the shortest confirmed in the set.
record_extra: Keys (unsettled)

Reported inconsistently after the 2019-21 renovation: 103 chambers and suites on the chateau's own site; 99 implied by French Wikipedia (28 rooms plus 71 suites); 108 in a 2021 trade article; 117 (the pre-renovation count of 57 suites and 60 rooms) still repeated in some press. No single figure was confirmed as authoritative -- airelles.com; fr.wikipedia.org; press, various.
Heritage

Built in the late nineteenth century as a wedding gift from Henry Brisson de la Messardiere to Louise Dupuy; restored and extended by architect Jean-Claude Rochette, then chief architect of France's Monuments Historiques, in 1989; awarded the 'Distinction Palace' label in June 2012. No monument-historique listing was found for the building itself -- fr.wikipedia.org.
Setting

A park of 12.5 hectares above Saint-Tropez per French Wikipedia; described elsewhere as 25 acres (about 10 hectares) -- the two figures are close and likely reflect rounding of the same grounds -- fr.wikipedia.org; luxurytraveladvisor.com.
Ownership

Owned by the Gibier family from 1992; bought by LOV Hotel Collection (Stephane Courbit's group, which also owns La Bastide de Gordes) in May 2019 for a reported EUR 154 million, financed in part by Cheyne Capital and Natixis; renovated under architect Christophe Tollemer and reopened as Airelles Saint-Tropez, Chateau de la Messardiere in July 2021 -- lhotellerie-restauration.fr; groupebpce.com; fr.wikipedia.org.
Wellness
A roughly 11,000 sq ft Valmont spa added in the 2019-21 renovation, with seven treatment rooms, a cryotherapy chamber, hammam, sauna, indoor pool and fitness centre -- luxurytraveladvisor.com.
Food and beverage
Five restaurants on the estate, including a culinary partnership with chef Nobu Matsuhisa -- fr.wikipedia.org; luxurytraveladvisor.com.
conflicts: The held capex basis (GBP 1.42m a key all-in, on the EUR 154m acquisition plus EUR 40m renovation over 117 keys, 2019-21) uses the pre-renovation key count. Post-renovation the operating key count is reported inconsistently: the chateau's own site states 103 chambers and suites; French Wikipedia implies 99 (28 rooms plus 71 suites); a 2021 trade article states 108; other press repeats the original 117. No single count was confirmed as authoritative. If the true operating count is closer to 103, capex a key is nearer GBP 1.88m rather than GBP 1.42m; at 99, nearer GBP 1.96m. This does not overturn the held figure, which is explicit about its 117-key basis, but the post-renovation denominator is unsettled.

chewton-glen.intro: Chewton Glen shares an ultimate owner with Cliveden House elsewhere in this set: Ian Livingstone bought it from its founders, Martin and Brigitte Skan, in 2006, and both hotels now sit inside Iconic Luxury Hotels, part of London and Regional Group Hotels Ltd. Where Cliveden's accounts are a mature, unchanging trading history, Chewton Glen's show a business still being actively reshaped by its owner, most recently through a going-concern refinancing due in September 2026. It is the reference in this set for what a continuously reinvested UK country house estate earns, costs to run and borrows against, on a full set of audited FY2024 accounts rather than a single conversion budget.
record: New Milton, Hampshire, on the edge of the New Forest National Park, a short walk from the sea; the hotel's own material states 130 acres of woodland, gardens and parkland

Reported inconsistently across sources as 70 to 72 keys in total: a main house of 58 rooms and suites, separate Coach House suites, and a set of treehouse suites in the grounds most recently marketed as 14 (earlier and some current sources give 12)

No Historic England listing was found for the main house under 'Chewton Glen' or 'Chewton Glen House'; unlike Cliveden, Heckfield Place and Estelle Manor in this set, it does not appear to be a statutorily listed building

Bought by Ian Livingstone from the Skan family in 2006 (reported price not confirmed); held via Chewton Glen Hotels Limited (company 00864881), a wholly owned subsidiary of London and Regional Group Hotels Ltd; ultimate controlling parties I M and R J Livingstone; a director (A Stembridge) also sits on the board of Iconic Luxury Hotels Limited
The treehouse suites were built by Blue Forest from 2012; one source (hotelplanner.com) gives a build cost of £7m for that phase; no total historical capital cost for the estate is published

FY2024 filed turnover £21.83m, down 3.3% on FY2023's £22.59m. Operating profit £4.27m (19.6% of turnover; FY2023 £4.14m, 18.3%). Profit before tax fell to £401k (FY2023: £2.98m) as interest payable rose from £1.20m to £3.90m on the company's Santander loan. Profit for the year £37k (FY2023: £2.88m). Payroll £7.53m = 34.5% of turnover (FY2023: 32.9%), on 321 average monthly employees (282 hotel and operations, 39 management and administration). Net assets £5.47m at 31 December 2024, after a £32.4m dividend paid to the group in 2023. The FY2024 accounts disclose a material uncertainty over going concern: a loan covenant was breached at 31 March 2025 (waived and reset), and the Santander facility (44,744k, 3-month SONIA plus 3.15%, secured on the freehold) is due for refinancing in September 2026
A spa with a 17-metre indoor lap pool, a hydrotherapy pool (13 jet stations), steam rooms and 12 treatment rooms; a separate outdoor pool; a nine-hole, par-3 golf course

Two restaurants: The Dining Room (fine dining, in a glasshouse extension) and The Kitchen (chef James Martin, informal, produce from the estate's kitchen garden); no Michelin star or Key confirmed from a Michelin Guide page directly (the page returned an access error)

Exclusive-use hire of the main house closes the restaurant and lounge to non-residents while all 58 main-house rooms and the treehouse suites remain available; capacity up to 140 for dining and 200 standing; weddings advertised from £9,800 for a weekday in June, food and drink included
cards: What happened

Ian Livingstone bought Chewton Glen from its founders, Martin and Brigitte Skan, in 2006; the reported price was not confirmed by Livingstone and no figure could be independently verified from a source I could open. It became part of what is now Iconic Luxury Hotels, alongside Cliveden House elsewhere in this set. The estate has grown since through continuous reinvestment in a trading hotel rather than a single conversion programme: a nine-hole golf course, a second restaurant (The Kitchen, with chef James Martin), and from 2012 a set of treehouse suites built by Blue Forest, later extended from an initial six lodges toward the 12 to 14 suites now marketed.
What it earns

FY2024 filed turnover was £21.83m, down 3.3% on FY2023's £22.59m; operating profit held at £4.27m, 19.6% of turnover. Profit before tax collapsed to £401k (FY2023: £2.98m) as interest payable nearly quadrupled to £3.90m, and profit for the year was £37k. Payroll ran at 34.5% of turnover (FY2023: 32.9%), on 321 average monthly employees. The company's own accounts flag a material uncertainty over going concern: its Santander facility is due for refinancing in September 2026, following a loan covenant breach in March 2025 that was waived and reset. Net assets stood at £5.47m, after a £32.4m dividend paid to the group in 2023.
What it evidences for Fawley

Chewton Glen's payroll runs at 34.5% of turnover, filed and audited, against Fawley's own 22.4%, but the two sit on different bases: Chewton Glen's is total staff cost over total revenue, and Fawley's is direct departmental wages only, before undistributed cost centres are added. On a like basis Chewton Glen is the heavier-staffed of the two. Its refinancing timing is the more transferable point: a mature, profitable hotel with a filed £4.27m operating profit and a facility due September 2026, already through one covenant breach, still carries real refinancing risk in this market — and Fawley's own refinancing is sized for the same year.
against: 70–72 across the main house, Coach House and treehouse suites (source count varies)
Chewton Glen's figure is total filed turnover across an uncertain key count; Fawley's is modelled year-7 revenue on a confirmed 60 keys.
26.3% EBITDA (£5.74m = operating profit £4.27m + depreciation £1.47m, FY2024, filed) / 19.6% operating profit margin after depreciation
EBITDA and GOP are different lines in the P&L waterfall: GOP sits above undistributed overheads and depreciation, EBITDA below them. This is not a like-for-like comparison.
Not computable on a like basis
The model does not split undistributed costs (A&G, S&M, POM) into wages and expenses, so a like-basis all-staff payroll percentage is not computable for the subject.
Santander facility due September 2026, after a covenant breach in March 2025 (waived and reset)
Same calendar window, different lender, structure and loan-to-value; a market-timing parallel, not a matched figure.

cliveden-house.intro: Cliveden sits on the same reach of the Thames as Fawley Court, eight miles downstream, and has traded as a hotel for four decades under a 100-year National Trust lease. It shares an ultimate owner with Chewton Glen elsewhere in this set: London and Regional, which bought the Cliveden lease in February 2012. Its filed accounts are a mature, audited trading history rather than a conversion story, and in October 2024 it became one of the first hotels in the UK to hold Two MICHELIN Keys, a hotel-stay rating distinct from a restaurant star. It is the reference point in this set for what a proven Thames-side country house actually earns once the ramp is over.

coworth-park.intro: Coworth Park occupies a Georgian estate outside Ascot, one of ten Dorchester Collection hotels owned through the Brunei Investment Agency, and the only one of the group's properties with its own polo grounds. It is a Dorchester Collection filing within a wider group, so what is publicly disclosed sits at the level of its own UK operating company rather than the group above it: full statutory accounts, filed and audited, name the exact trading result. It belongs in this set as the closest UK trading analogue to Fawley on structure, a converted country house with an equestrian offer and a Michelin-starred restaurant, and it is the one hotel in the whole cohort whose filed accounts show a loss rather than a profit.
record: 240 acres of parkland in Ascot, Berkshire, Dorchester Collection's own stated figure; Michelin's own listing gives 246 acres, so the precise surveyed extent is not independently established. The grounds include a wildflower meadow, the Lime Grove, rose gardens, a croquet lawn, woodland trails, a lake and two professional polo fields

71 rooms and suites (49 rooms, 22 suites): 30 in the Mansion House, 30 in the converted Stables, 9 in the Cottages, plus two separately named signature suites, the Dower House and North Lodge. An earlier Dorchester factsheet states 70 rooms and suites plus two signature suites, a minor inconsistency in the operator's own material rather than a portal conflict
The Dower House (1755) and North Lodge are each Grade II listed; the main house dates to 1776, built for the East India merchant William Shepheard

Prince Jefri acquired the estate in 1995 and it transferred to the Brunei Investment Agency in 2001. Restoration into a hotel began in 2008; the property opened in September 2010 as Dorchester Collection's eighth hotel. Conversion architect EPR Architects, interior design Fox Linton Associates, spa designed by Purcell

£23m, the only disclosed development-cost figure, stated by the project's structural engineer rather than by Dorchester Collection or the Brunei Investment Agency; a project-source estimate, not an audited owner disclosure

Filed average room rate of £676.0 in FY2024, down £41 (-6%) on FY2023, alongside filed occupancy of 62.4%, up 3.8 percentage points year on year. This is a filed annual average, on a different basis from the portal's held lead-in bookable rate of £650 gross, £542 net

FY2024 filed revenue £21.615m (Rooms £10.3m, Food & Beverage £7.8m, other £3.5m), an operating loss of £3.181m and a net loss of £3.663m; FY2023 revenue £21.107m and a net loss of £3.191m. Net liabilities of £59.466m at 31 December 2024, with the going-concern basis resting explicitly on continuing support from the ultimate parent, the Brunei Investment Agency
Average 229 employees in FY2024 (210 operations, 19 administration); aggregate payroll cost £8.693m, 40.2% of revenue

An on-site equestrian centre offers riding, private lessons and hacks. Guards Polo Club manages Coworth Park's two polo fields and runs the on-site Guards Polo Academy. 40 stables were specified at the 2010 launch; no current published count was found

The Spa at Coworth Park: eight treatment rooms, a heated indoor pool, sauna, steam room and gym. Floor area reported as 1,300 sqm across two floors in a 2015 trade profile, not confirmed by the current operator

Woven by Adam Smith holds one Michelin star, awarded in 2023, succeeding Restaurant Coworth Park's 2018 star. Other outlets are The Barn, the Drawing Room, The Bar, the Spa Café and the seasonal terrace TIDE. The hotel separately holds two Michelin Keys, a distinct award from the restaurant star
Four spaces: Oval Room, Garden Room, Oak Room and Tower House, with a largest published seated dinner capacity of 100. Exclusive-use hire is offered with pricing on request; no rate is published
cards: What happened

Coworth House dates to 1776, built for the East India merchant William Shepheard, and passed through a series of owners including the Earl of Derby before Selfridges and Fortnum & Mason's owner Galen Weston bought the estate in the mid-1980s and built its first polo ground. Prince Jefri acquired it in 1995 and it transferred to the Brunei Investment Agency in 2001. Restoration into a hotel began in 2008 and the property opened in September 2010 as Dorchester Collection's eighth hotel, with EPR Architects converting the buildings and Fox Linton Associates designing the interiors. The only disclosed development cost, £23m, comes from the project's structural engineer rather than from Dorchester Collection itself, so it should be read as a project-source estimate rather than an audited figure.
What it earns

Coworth Park is the only hotel in this comparable set with full, filed, audited UK statutory accounts, and they show a hotel trading at a loss. FY2024 revenue was £21.615m against an average room rate of £676 and 62.4% occupancy; the company made an operating loss of £3.181m and a net loss of £3.663m, a continuation of the prior year's loss. Payroll averaged 229 employees and cost £8.693m, 40.2% of revenue. Net liabilities stood at £59.466m at the 2024 year end, and the auditors' going-concern opinion rests explicitly on continuing support from the ultimate parent, the Brunei Investment Agency.
What it evidences for Fawley

Coworth Park is the closest UK trading analogue to Fawley on structure: a converted Georgian country house with a polo and equestrian offer, a Michelin-starred restaurant, and year-round trading, and it is losing money at an occupancy of 62.4%, close to Fawley's own 65% stabilised assumption. Its 40.2% payroll ratio, on a fully loaded filed basis that includes administration, sits well above the 22.4% direct-departmental-wages figure the Fawley model carries; the two are not on the same basis, but the gap is a caution on how much cost a comparable property carries outside departmental lines. A UK country-house hotel of comparable ambition running at a loss, fourteen years into trading, is the sharpest single data point this cohort holds against Fawley's underwritten margin.

Coworth's is a bottom-line UK GAAP operating result after all administration and lease costs, not a GOP figure on the same USALI basis as Fawley's; the two measures are structurally different, but the sign, a loss against an underwritten profit, is the useful fact

estelle-manor.intro: Estelle Manor sits in this set for its club engine, not its rate: the portal carries no bookable rate year for the property, but its FY2025 filed accounts show 618 employees at 5.72 a key and a members' club charging £3,600 a year plus a £500 joining fee. The Grade II mansion already traded as a 135-room hotel, Eynsham Hall, before Ennismore bought it in 2018 — reported at an asking price of £8.25m — and reopened it as Estelle Manor in spring 2023. Its 49.5% payroll ratio and negative EBITDA margin are the sharpest illustration in the cohort of what a full-service club-and-hotel staffing model costs to run.

A 60-acre estate near Eynsham, Oxfordshire, on the edge of the Cotswolds, within roughly 3,000 acres of surrounding parkland

The property traded as the 135-bedroom Eynsham Hall country house hotel before the 2018 sale. Eynsham Baths: a 3,000 sq m Roman-inspired spa with a tepidarium bathing hall, five pools, a tea lounge and ten treatment rooms including a dedicated Ceremony Suite

Five outlets: the Brasserie, a traditional Chinese restaurant, the Billiards Room, the Glasshouse and the Armoury (Japanese)

gleneagles.intro: Gleneagles sits on 850 acres of Perthshire parkland built around three golf courses, the largest and most institutionally owned property in the comparable set. Diageo held the estate for thirty-one years before selling it in 2015 to a consortium led by Ennismore, the group behind The Hoxton, which has run it since. It carries the set's only disclosed acquisition yield and the deepest run of filed trading accounts of any comparable, at a scale — 232 keys against Fawley Court's 60 — that makes it a scale-and-mix check on the underwrite rather than a like-for-like one.
record: Auchterarder, Perthshire; 850 acres including three golf courses (the King's and Queen's Courses, both designed by James Braid, and the Jack Nicklaus-designed PGA Centenary Course, host of the 2014 Ryder Cup), formal gardens and equestrian ground
232, comprising around 205 bedrooms across four categories (Estate Rooms in the Main House and in Braid House, Manor Rooms, Country Rooms) and 27 suites, all in the Main House
Category B listed (Historic Environment Scotland, LB4570, designated 8 April 1980); also entered in the Inventory of Gardens and Designed Landscapes in Scotland (1 July 1987)

Opened 1924, built by the Caledonian Railway; passed through British Transport Hotels, Gleneagles Hotels plc, Arthur Bell & Sons and Guinness before thirty-one years under Diageo (1984–2015); sold by Diageo to a private investment group led by Ennismore in July 2015, held since via GH Holdings 2 Limited (company 9627840, over 75% of shares and voting rights, notified to Companies House 6 April 2016)

Filed by Gleneagles Hotels Limited (company SC097000): turnover £43.5m and operating profit £2.6m in the last full year under Diageo (year to 30 June 2014); turnover £51.2m and operating profit £2.5m for the year to 31 December 2017; turnover £55.3m and operating profit £3.5m for the year to 31 December 2018. The accounting period then moved to 31 March: a 15-month period to March 2020 closed on £66.4m turnover, a £5.2m pre-tax loss and 967 employees as the pandemic shut the hotel; the year to March 2022 recovered to £68.9m turnover and a £7.0m pre-tax profit
The Spa by ESPA: 20 treatment rooms, two indoor pools, an outdoor thermal pool, a hydrotherapy pool, sauna, steam room and gym

The British School of Falconry, founded 1982 and relocated to the estate in 1992; the Gleneagles Equestrian School, a 50-acre British Horse Society-accredited site with 26 horses and ponies; gun dog training and shooting instruction; off-road driving

Six restaurants (Strathearn, Restaurant Andrew Fairlie, Birnam Brasserie, The Dormy, Glendevon, the Garden Café) and four bars; Restaurant Andrew Fairlie opened 2001 and has held two Michelin stars since 2006, Scotland's longest-standing two-star restaurant
A ballroom and multiple function rooms; weddings are resident-only, so all guests stay on the estate; no maximum capacity is published

Golf membership: Individual £3,780 a year plus £2,000 joining, with categories from £645 (Junior, 13–17) to £14,617 + VAT (Corporate). A separate 33-key members' hotel, Gleneagles Townhouse, opened in Edinburgh in June 2022 (£2,200 a year plus £350 joining, or £1,100/£175 under 33) — an Ennismore-Gleneagles property, not part of the 232-key estate
cards: What happened

Gleneagles opened in 1924, built by the Caledonian Railway as a golfing hotel beside its own station, and passed through British Transport Hotels and a run of drinks groups — Arthur Bell & Sons, then Guinness, then Diageo — from 1984 to 2015. Diageo sold the estate to a private investment group led by Ennismore in July 2015, for a price analysts put at £150–180m, retaining existing management and committing to a multi-million-pound refurbishment programme; no absolute spend figure has been published. The renovation reached the bedrooms, a new Birnam Brasserie and a creche, and turnover rose in each of the two years first reported afterwards.
What it earns

Gleneagles Hotels Limited (SC097000) files standalone accounts at Companies House. Turnover rose from £51.2m to £55.3m between the years ended December 2017 and 2018, with operating profit up from £2.5m to £3.5m — a 4.9% to 6.3% operating margin, computed after depreciation on the full P&L, not a GOP or EBITDA line. A 15-month period to March 2020 closed on £66.4m turnover, a £5.2m pre-tax loss and 967 employees as the pandemic shut the hotel; the year to March 2022 recovered to £68.9m turnover and a £7.0m pre-tax profit.
What it evidences for Fawley

At 232 keys Gleneagles trades at nearly four times Fawley Court's proposed scale, and its FY2018 turnover of £55.3m implies about £238k of revenue a key against Fawley's underwritten £756k — a function of scale and mix rather than rate, since Gleneagles' own lead-in (£750 gross) sits below the £1,000 underwritten here. Its 6.3% operating margin is a fully loaded, post-depreciation figure and is not comparable to Fawley's 33.96% GOP; the two sit on different lines of the P&L. It is the only comparable in the set with a disclosed acquisition yield — 5.50% in 2015 — evidence for the buy side of the underwrite rather than the operate side.

heckfield-place.intro: Heckfield Place is the slowest, least commercial UK conversion in this set: Gerald Chan, a Boston-based investor, bought the Grade II manor in 2002 and spent close to a decade rebuilding it around a working farm rather than a fixed opening date, welcoming guests only in September 2018. No ownership structure isolates a property-level profit and loss account, so the payroll figure the portal already carries is modelled rather than filed, the only unfiled figure among the UK comparables in this set. Its two farm-fed restaurants and its 17,000 sq ft spa show what a patient, estate-led conversion looks like once it is finally open and trading.
record_extra: Setting (detail)
A 438-acre estate including a working biodynamic Home Farm, dairy, Market Garden and ancient woodland (the portal's own record does not currently carry an acreage figure)
Ownership (detail)

hotel-du-cap-eden-roc.intro: Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc occupies the tip of the Cap d'Antibes, in a nine-hectare park between Cannes and Nice, and has traded as a hotel since 1889. The Oetker family has owned it since 1969 and it now anchors the Oetker Collection. It sits in the comparable set as the one property whose rate, even measured on its thinnest and cheapest available window, sits above Fawley's underwritten ADR - a useful ceiling reading, even though the hotel discloses almost nothing else publicly and trades roughly half the year Fawley underwrites.
record: Cap d'Antibes, on the French Riviera between Cannes and Nice, in a park reported at nine hectares (antibesjuanlespins.com) or around 22 acres of gardens (press descriptions); both figures are carried since neither is clearly primary (en.wikipedia.org; oetkerhotels.com).

111 guestrooms per the hotel's own site, across the original Villa Soleil, the Eden-Roc Pavilion and the private Les Deux Fontaines residence; other press sources give 117 or 118, unreconciled. Four further rental villas sit in the gardens (oetkerhotels.com; press conflict noted).

Built in 1869 as the private Villa Soleil for Hippolyte de Villemessant, founder of Le Figaro; bought and renovated by hotelier Antoine Sella, who reopened it as the Grand Hotel du Cap in January 1889; the Eden Roc pavilion, about 400 yards from the main house, was added in 1914. No formal heritage listing or monument protection was found for the buildings (en.wikipedia.org; oetkerhotels.com history page).

Already held: 20 April to 18 October, about six months, from trade listings for the current season. Our own booking-engine collection only returned 20 bookable nights, all between 28 September and 17 October 2026, with nothing loaded beyond 18 October - too thin a window to test the held season figure directly, but consistent with it (already held; own rate collection).

Bought by Rudolph August Oetker in 1969 from Antoine Sella's family, who were reportedly seeking a buyer who shared their approach to the hotel; it has remained in Oetker family ownership since and now sits within Oetker Collection (oetkerhotels.com history page; press synthesis).

No figure was found for the 1969 acquisition. Press reports on subsequent renovation spend conflict: a USD 67m programme reported for 2011, a EUR 45m programme reported for 2008-15, and a separate account of a seven-year refurbishment completed around 2013 - including new plumbing and electrics for the original Villa Soleil building and the creation of the Eden-Roc Grill and Champagne Lounge - costed at over EUR 60m. None of the three is filed or primary (press synthesis, multiple conflicting sources).
No revenue, margin, payroll or occupancy figure was found. No single-entity French filing for the hotel was located in this research, and Oetker Collection does not disclose property-level results.
A Dior-branded spa (press and hotel-site references; treatment-room count and spa area not found).

Three restaurants: Eden-Roc restaurant, Louroc (one Michelin star) and Le Grill. The hotel itself holds Three MICHELIN Keys in the Michelin Guide's hotel classification (whatahotel.com; guide.michelin.com).
Not found - no wedding, meeting or buyout capacity was located in the accessible record.
None for sale. Four rental villas in the gardens and the separate Les Deux Fontaines residence are let as accommodation, not sold as freehold or leasehold units (oetkerhotels.com).
cards: What happened

The house began in 1869 as a private mansion, Villa Soleil, built for the founder of Le Figaro. Hotelier Antoine Sella bought and renovated it, reopening as the Grand Hotel du Cap in January 1889; the separate Eden Roc pavilion, about 400 yards along the coast, followed in 1914. The Oetker family bought the hotel in 1969 and has owned it since, through what is now Oetker Collection. Press accounts describe a further seven-year renovation programme completing around 2013-15, variously costed at USD 67m, EUR 45m or over EUR 60m depending on the source, none of them filed or primary.
What it earns

Nothing is published. No single-entity French accounts for the hotel were located in this research and Oetker Collection does not disclose property-level trading figures, so no revenue, margin, payroll or occupancy number exists for this property in the accessible record.
What it evidences for Fawley

Eden-Roc is the one comparable in the whole cohort whose collected rate sits above Fawley's GBP 1,000 underwritten ADR - GBP 1,329 gross even on its cheapest available nights. But the collection is thin: only 20 nights were bookable at all, confined to a 19-day window in late September and October, with the actual summer peak never loaded for sale, so this should be read as a floor rather than a fair annual average. The season is the sharper transferable point: at roughly six months a year, even the hotel most confident of its own pricing power in this entire set does not attempt anything close to Fawley's 365-day calendar.
